children: By Barbara Kollmeyer
BNY Mellon manager bets on utilities and energy pipelines
BNY Mellon Global Infrastructure Income exchange-traded fund manager Brock Campbell says the artificial-intelligence theme has been exciting, but it's far from over.
Fund manager Brock Campbell jokes that his children would "give up both electricity and water to have access to Roblox."

Kidding aside, the manager of the BNY Mellon Global Infrastructure Income ETF BKGI sees telecommunications and data as vital basic needs. "These are things you're not just going to cut off when the economy weakens, and that's a fantastic opportunity to introduce ballast into a portfolio," Campbell told MarketWatch in a recent interview.

His five-star Morningstar rated fund has returned 21% on a three-year annualized basis, beating a 16% gain for its benchmark S&P Global Infrastructure Index. Assets under management for the four-year-old ETF totaled $1.9 billion as of Sept. 21, more than tripling from $640 million when MarketWatch spoke to Campbell in February.
"Infrastructure offers diversification, downside protection, and inflation protection that are particularly appealing in today's environment of elevated geopolitical uncertainty," he said.

Investors have also likely been drawn to artificial intelligence, which has proved a catalyst for the sector that suffered a decades-long trough amid stagnation of U.S. electricity consumption. Campbell described a "lightbulb" moment for his team in late 2022, when ChatGPT debuted and they realized how power hungry next-generation AI chips would be.

"We hadn't had a growth market in infrastructure in 30 to 40 years," he said. "That was a catalyst for us to start thinking about supply chains, and since then we've spent a lot of time thinking about pinch points into that supply chain."

He was drawn to power generators - historically very cyclical - that looked stable and defensive, yet exciting given the potential to "sign deals with data centers at high prices." The fund picked up Dominion Energy (D) in late 2022. Earlier this year, NextEra Energy (NEE) announced a $67 billion merger with the power and energy group.

Campbell said they are increasingly focused, though, on a U.S. shift toward using natural gas in data centers. "We fundamentally believe there is going to be a massive build-out of new natural gas-fired facilities, and in order for those facilities to run, you need the pipelines to connect to them."

Given how hard it is to build new ones, they look for companies with "world-class existing pipelines" that can build smaller connecting ones to service new gas plants. Major player Hess Midstream (HESM) is the fund's top holding.
"In the U.S., we don't believe that excitement has come through, so we think that's an area where investors could benefit from the AI buildup," he said.

Pipelines are also a play on energy security, a theme that has strengthened amid the outbreak of the Iran war, he said. "Clearly infrastructure plays a critical role in both the electrification side, but also on the oil- and natural-gas pipeline side."

Campbell said they've been rotating out of U.S. utilities and into regional European players. While Europe's regulatory road for data centers will likely be tougher, "the first pinch point is going to be access to power," he said. Finnish utility provider Fortum (FI:FORTUM), a holding in the fund, recently signed a long-term electricity deal with Alphabet's Google (GOOGL) to expand the latter's European AI reach.
Among the fund's top holdings are Spain's Naturgy Energy (ES:NTGY), Bouygues (FR:EN) and Engie (FR:ENGI) of France.

"Our team has a thesis around data sovereignty, i.e., you need a localization of data center build-out for data security. We believe that Europe was going to have to eventually replicate and we're at the very early innings of that replication," he said.

He dismissed fears by some investors that the AI cycle could be waning after a period of intense excitement. "We haven't even scratched the surface, infrastructure is a long, long tail. It takes a long time for regulatory approval for building and then obviously deploying."
Tools like agentic AI have a huge demand for power, Campbell said. "The compute just feels insatiable to me, I don't see any end in sight."
